questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The visual art element referring to a continuous mark made on a surface, used to define edges or create movement, is called
questions.explanation: Line is one of the most fundamental art elements, used to define contours, create patterns, and suggest movement or direction.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The visual art element referring to a two-dimensional, flat, enclosed area is called
questions.explanation: Shape is a two-dimensional element, defined by boundaries such as lines or changes in colour or value.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The visual art element referring to a three-dimensional object having volume, such as a sphere or cube, is called
questions.explanation: Form describes three-dimensional objects, possessing height, width, and depth, unlike flat two-dimensional shapes.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The visual art element concerned with hues such as red, blue, and yellow, produced by light reflecting off a surface, is called
questions.explanation: Colour refers to the hues perceived from reflected light, one of the most expressive elements in visual art.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The visual art element describing the surface quality of an object, such as rough, smooth, or bumpy, is called
questions.explanation: Texture refers to the surface quality of an artwork or object, which may be actual (tactile) or implied (visual).

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The visual art element referring to the area around, between, or within objects in an artwork is called
questions.explanation: Space refers to the area occupied by, or surrounding, objects or forms within an artwork, including positive and negative space.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The visual art element referring to the lightness or darkness of a colour or tone is called
questions.explanation: Value describes the relative lightness or darkness of a colour, essential for creating contrast and the illusion of form.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The organising principle of art concerned with the equal or harmonious distribution of visual weight in a composition is called
questions.explanation: Balance refers to how visual weight is distributed within a composition, whether symmetrically, asymmetrically, or radially.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The organising principle of art concerned with the repetition of elements to create a sense of organised movement is called
questions.explanation: Rhythm is created through the repetition or alternation of elements, producing a sense of visual movement and flow.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The organising principle of art concerned with the relative size relationships between different parts of a composition is called
questions.explanation: Proportion concerns the relative size and scale relationships among elements within a composition.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The organising principle of art concerned with placing differing elements together to highlight their differences is called
questions.explanation: Contrast juxtaposes differing elements, such as light and dark, or rough and smooth, to create visual interest and tension.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The organising principle of art concerned with drawing attention to a particular focal point within a composition is called
questions.explanation: Emphasis directs the viewer's attention to a specific area or element considered the focal point of the artwork.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The organising principle of art concerned with creating a sense of wholeness and cohesion among all elements in a composition is called
questions.explanation: Unity refers to the sense that all elements in a composition work together cohesively as a harmonious whole.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The organising principle of art concerned with introducing difference and diversity to avoid monotony in a composition is called
questions.explanation: Variety introduces diverse elements into a composition, preventing it from becoming monotonous or overly repetitive.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A composition in which both sides of a central axis mirror each other closely is described as having
questions.explanation: Symmetrical balance occurs when elements are mirrored evenly on either side of a central axis, creating a formal, stable composition.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A composition in which visual weight is balanced using differing elements on either side, rather than mirrored elements, is described as having
questions.explanation: Asymmetrical balance achieves visual equilibrium through varied elements of differing size, colour, or shape rather than exact mirroring.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A composition in which elements radiate outward from a central point is described as having
questions.explanation: Radial balance arranges elements so that they emanate outward from a central focal point, as seen in wheel-like or circular designs.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The illusion of a third dimension (depth) created on a flat, two-dimensional surface is achieved primarily through the element of
questions.explanation: Space, through techniques like overlapping and perspective, creates the illusion of depth and distance on a flat surface.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A gradual, evenly increasing or decreasing change in the size, colour, or spacing of elements within a composition is called a
questions.explanation: Gradation involves a gradual, step-by-step change in a visual element, creating a sense of smooth transition or movement.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The visual illusion of texture created through drawing or painting techniques, without any actual physical surface variation, is called
questions.explanation: Implied texture is rendered visually to suggest a surface quality, without the artwork's surface physically possessing that texture.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The colours red, yellow, and blue, from which all other colours can theoretically be mixed, are called
questions.explanation: Primary colours (red, yellow, blue) are the foundational colours that cannot be created by mixing other colours together.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: Colours created by mixing two primary colours together, such as green, orange, and purple, are called
questions.explanation: Secondary colours (green, orange, purple) result from mixing pairs of primary colours in equal proportions.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: Colours created by mixing a primary colour with an adjacent secondary colour, such as red-orange, are called
questions.explanation: Tertiary colours result from mixing a primary colour with a neighbouring secondary colour on the colour wheel.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: Colours positioned directly opposite each other on the colour wheel, such as red and green, are called
questions.explanation: Complementary colours sit opposite one another on the colour wheel, and when placed together create strong visual contrast.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: Colours located next to each other on the colour wheel, sharing a common hue, are called
questions.explanation: Analogous colours are neighbouring hues on the colour wheel, producing a harmonious, cohesive colour scheme.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A colour scheme built from a single hue, varied only through changes in value (lightness/darkness) or intensity, is called
questions.explanation: A monochromatic colour scheme uses variations of a single hue, adjusting only its lightness or saturation.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: Colours such as red, orange, and yellow, often associated with heat, fire, and energy, are classified as
questions.explanation: Warm colours (reds, oranges, yellows) evoke feelings of warmth, energy, and closeness in visual compositions.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: Colours such as blue, green, and violet, often associated with calmness, water, and distance, are classified as
questions.explanation: Cool colours (blues, greens, violets) evoke feelings of calmness, coolness, and distance in visual compositions.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The visual diagram arranging colours in a circular format to show their relationships is called the
questions.explanation: The colour wheel organises primary, secondary, and tertiary colours in a circular arrangement, illustrating their relationships.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: Mixing a colour with white to lighten it produces a
questions.explanation: A tint is created by adding white to a pure colour, lightening its value.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The archaeological art culture discovered in central Nigeria, famous for its terracotta sculptures dating back over 2,000 years, is the
questions.explanation: The Nok culture, centred on the Jos Plateau, is renowned for producing some of Africa's earliest known terracotta sculptures.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The ancient Yoruba art culture famous for its naturalistic bronze and terracotta heads, regarded as the spiritual origin of Yoruba art, is
questions.explanation: Ife art is celebrated for its remarkably naturalistic bronze and terracotta heads, reflecting a highly refined sculptural tradition.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The art culture famous for its sophisticated lost-wax bronze casting under royal patronage, associated with the Oba's court, is the
questions.explanation: Benin art, closely tied to the royal court of the Oba, is renowned for its elaborate bronze plaques and sculptures made using the lost-wax casting method.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The archaeological site in south-eastern Nigeria known for elaborately decorated bronze artefacts dated to around the 9th century is
questions.explanation: Igbo-Ukwu is celebrated for its intricately decorated bronze objects, demonstrating advanced metalworking skill centuries before European contact.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The Nigerian art site famous for its collection of hundreds of soapstone (steatite) figures depicting seated human forms is
questions.explanation: Esie in present-day Kwara State is known for its large collection of carved soapstone figures, whose exact origins remain a subject of study.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The Nigerian art culture geographically and stylistically positioned between Ife and Benin, known for its own terracotta and ivory carving traditions, is
questions.explanation: Owo art shares stylistic connections with both Ife and Benin traditions, reflecting its geographic position between the two centres.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The medium most closely associated with the Nok culture's sculptural output is
questions.explanation: Nok sculptures were predominantly made of terracotta, fired clay figures notable for their distinctive stylised features.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The medium most closely associated with the Ife and Benin cultures' most celebrated sculptural works is
questions.explanation: Ife and Benin are especially renowned for their bronze castings, produced using the sophisticated lost-wax (cire perdue) method.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The medium most closely associated with the Esie sculptural collection is
questions.explanation: The Esie figures are carved from soapstone, a soft stone that allowed for detailed, though weathering-prone, sculptural work.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A key stylistic characteristic of Ife sculpture, distinguishing it from many other early African art traditions, is its
options: complete absence of the human figure
extreme abstraction with no human resemblance
naturalism, depicting lifelike human proportions and features
exclusive use of geometric patterns only
questions.explanation: Ife sculpture is particularly noted for its striking naturalism, portraying the human face and form with lifelike accuracy and proportion.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A key stylistic characteristic of Benin bronze plaques is their frequent depiction of
options: royal court scenes, the Oba, and chiefs in ceremonial regalia
questions.explanation: Benin bronze plaques commonly depict the Oba, chiefs, and court life, serving as historical records of the kingdom's royal history.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A key stylistic characteristic of Nok terracotta sculpture is its distinctive
options: stylised facial features, especially large, detailed eyes
use of glass and metal exclusively
questions.explanation: Nok sculptures are recognisable for their distinctively stylised features, particularly large, elaborately detailed eyes.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The traditional Nigerian art cultures (Nok, Ife, Benin, Igbo-Ukwu, Esie, Owo) are collectively important to art history because they demonstrate
options: the complete absence of artistic tradition in pre-colonial Nigeria
sophisticated artistic and technical skill in Africa well before significant European contact
a single unified style with no regional variation
art forms entirely imported from Europe
questions.explanation: These archaeological art cultures collectively demonstrate that highly sophisticated artistic and technical traditions existed in Nigeria long before European colonisation.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The lost-wax (cire perdue) casting method, used extensively in Ife and Benin art, involves
options: creating a wax model that is coated in clay, then melted out and replaced with molten metal
carving directly into solid metal with chisels
weaving metal threads into a textile pattern
painting a design directly onto a finished metal surface
questions.explanation: Lost-wax casting involves sculpting a model in wax, encasing it in clay, then melting out the wax and pouring in molten metal to fill the resulting cavity.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The traditional Nigerian art cultures are typically studied and dated by art historians using methods such as
options: reliance solely on oral tradition with no physical evidence
comparison with only European art of the same period
questions.explanation: Archaeologists and art historians date and study these cultures through careful excavation, along with analysis of stylistic features and materials used.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A key reason the Benin bronzes are significant to art historians beyond their aesthetic value is that they
options: depict only imported European subjects with no local content
were produced entirely without royal patronage or oversight
serve as historical records documenting Benin's royal court, rulers, and important events
were created using materials found nowhere in Africa
questions.explanation: Beyond their artistic merit, Benin bronzes function as visual historical documents, recording rulers, ceremonies, and significant events of the kingdom.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The prehistoric cave in France famous for its extensive collection of Palaeolithic wall paintings depicting animals such as bulls and horses is
questions.explanation: Lascaux, in southwestern France, contains some of the most famous prehistoric cave paintings, depicting large animals in vivid detail.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The prehistoric cave in Spain renowned for its Palaeolithic paintings of bison, discovered in the 19th century, is
questions.explanation: Altamira in Spain is famous for its Palaeolithic cave paintings, particularly its striking depictions of bison.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: Prehistoric cave paintings such as those at Lascaux and Altamira were most likely created using
options: natural pigments such as charcoal and ochre
questions.explanation: Prehistoric artists used naturally available materials, such as charcoal and mineral-based ochre pigments, to create their cave paintings.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The Egyptian art convention depicting the human figure with the head and legs in profile but the torso and eye facing forward is called
questions.explanation: Egyptian art frequently used a composite (frontality) convention, combining profile and frontal views within a single figure to show the body's most recognisable aspects.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The massive stone tomb structures built for Egyptian pharaohs, most famously at Giza, are called
questions.explanation: Pyramids were monumental tomb structures built to house and protect the remains and treasures of Egyptian pharaohs.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: Carved or painted images found on the walls of Egyptian tombs, often depicting daily life, gods, and the afterlife, are called
questions.explanation: Tomb reliefs are carved (and often painted) images decorating the walls of Egyptian tombs, depicting scenes intended to accompany the deceased into the afterlife.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A key purpose of Egyptian funerary art, including pyramids and tomb reliefs, was to
options: support the pharaoh's journey into and life within the afterlife
serve no religious or spiritual purpose
questions.explanation: Much of Egyptian art served a religious and funerary function, intended to protect and sustain the deceased in their journey to the afterlife.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: Egyptian art is generally characterised by
options: constant, rapid stylistic change from one era to the next
complete abstraction with no recognisable figures
the total absence of religious subject matter
a strict adherence to established conventions and proportions over long periods
questions.explanation: Egyptian art followed established conventions of proportion and representation consistently over an unusually long period of its civilisation's history.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The tall, four-sided, tapering stone monuments erected by the ancient Egyptians, often inscribed with hieroglyphs, are called
questions.explanation: Obelisks are tall, tapering stone monuments, often commemorating pharaohs or gods, inscribed with hieroglyphic text.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The large stone statue near the Giza pyramids, combining a lion's body with a human (or pharaoh's) head, is called the
questions.explanation: The Great Sphinx of Giza combines a lion's body with a human head, believed to represent the pharaoh, guarding the pyramid complex.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The late 19th-century art movement characterised by loose brushwork and an emphasis on capturing light and momentary impressions, associated with artists like Monet, is
questions.explanation: Impressionism focused on capturing fleeting effects of light and colour with visible, loose brushstrokes, pioneered by artists such as Claude Monet.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The early 20th-century art movement characterised by fragmented, geometric forms depicting multiple viewpoints simultaneously, associated with Picasso and Braque, is
questions.explanation: Cubism broke objects into geometric fragments and depicted them from multiple angles at once, pioneered by Picasso and Braque.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The 20th-century art movement exploring the world of dreams, the unconscious mind, and irrational, fantastical imagery, associated with artists like Salvador Dalí, is
questions.explanation: Surrealism drew on dream imagery and the unconscious mind to create fantastical, often unsettling artworks, exemplified by Salvador Dalí.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The art movement characterised by works that do not attempt to represent recognisable subject matter, instead emphasising colour, form, and gesture, is
questions.explanation: Abstract art moves away from realistic representation, focusing instead on shapes, colours, and forms independent of recognisable subject matter.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: Which Nigerian artist is widely regarded as a pioneering modernist sculptor, celebrated for works blending African and Western artistic traditions?
questions.explanation: Ben Enwonwu was a pioneering Nigerian modernist artist, renowned for sculptures and paintings that fused African subject matter with Western artistic techniques.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: Which Nigerian artist is widely regarded as a founding figure of modern Nigerian art, pioneering the introduction of formal Western art education in Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Aina Onabolu is credited as a founding figure of modern Nigerian art, instrumental in introducing formal Western-style art education into Nigerian schools.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: Which Nigerian artist became internationally celebrated for her distinctive pottery, particularly large water pots decorated with traditional motifs?
questions.explanation: Ladi Kwali achieved international recognition for her skilfully crafted pottery, especially her large traditional water pots with incised decorative patterns.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: Which Nigerian artist is particularly celebrated for pioneering innovative printmaking techniques, including deep-etched relief prints?
questions.explanation: Bruce Onobrakpeya is renowned for his innovative printmaking, including his development of deep-etching techniques within relief printing.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: Modern and contemporary Nigerian art is often noted for its tendency to
options: completely reject any connection to traditional African art
avoid engaging with contemporary social or cultural themes
exclusively replicate ancient Nok, Ife, and Benin styles with no innovation
blend traditional African themes and motifs with modern or Western artistic techniques
questions.explanation: A recurring characteristic of modern Nigerian art is its fusion of traditional African subject matter and motifs with techniques and concepts drawn from Western art education.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A key distinguishing feature between Impressionism and Cubism is that Impressionism focused on
options: sculpture exclusively, while Cubism focused on painting only
religious subject matter exclusively, while Cubism focused on portraiture
capturing light and colour in a naturalistic scene, while Cubism fragmented forms into geometric shapes
purely geometric abstraction, while Cubism focused on natural light
questions.explanation: Impressionism aimed to capture natural light and atmosphere in recognisable scenes, whereas Cubism deconstructed subjects into fragmented geometric forms.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: Ben Enwonwu's most famous public sculpture, commissioned for Nigeria's independence-era House of Representatives, is titled
questions.explanation: Enwonwu's 'Anyanwu' ('Awakening'), a bronze sculpture symbolising the rising sun, is among his most celebrated and recognisable works.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: Modern Nigerian art education, formally introduced by pioneers such as Aina Onabolu, was significant because it
options: established structured Western-style art training within Nigerian schools for the first time
was solely focused on European subject matter with no local relevance
abolished all traditional Nigerian art practices immediately
had no lasting impact on later generations of Nigerian artists
questions.explanation: Onabolu's efforts were pivotal in introducing formal, structured Western art education into the Nigerian school curriculum, shaping generations of artists.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A drawing exercise involving the careful arrangement and rendering of inanimate objects, such as fruit or bottles, is called
questions.explanation: Still-life drawing involves carefully observing and rendering an arranged group of inanimate objects.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: Drawing exercises focused on natural subjects such as plants, trees, and outdoor scenery are broadly classified as
questions.explanation: Nature drawing covers subjects drawn directly from the natural environment, including plants, trees, and landscapes.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: Drawing exercises focused on capturing the human body's proportions, gestures, and anatomy are broadly classified as
questions.explanation: Figure drawing focuses specifically on depicting the human body accurately, including proportion, gesture, and anatomical structure.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A dry drawing medium made from compressed carbon, producing rich, dark tones and easily smudged for shading, is
questions.explanation: Charcoal is a versatile dry drawing medium prized for its deep, rich blacks and ease of blending for tonal shading.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A soft drawing medium made of pigment mixed with a binder, available in stick form and often used for vibrant colour blending, is
questions.explanation: Pastels are sticks of pigment bound together, allowing for direct, vibrant colour application and blending.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A painting medium using pigment suspended in water, known for its transparency and delicate washes, is
questions.explanation: Watercolour paint is prized for its transparent quality, allowing light to reflect through thin washes of colour.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A painting medium similar to watercolour but formulated to be opaque rather than transparent is
questions.explanation: Gouache is a water-based paint similar to watercolour, but made opaque through the addition of a white pigment or higher pigment concentration.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A fast-drying, water-based painting medium known for its versatility and durability once dry is
questions.explanation: Acrylic paint dries quickly and can be applied thickly or thinly, offering versatility across different painting techniques.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: When drawing the human figure, understanding the underlying skeletal and muscular structure is part of studying
questions.explanation: Anatomical study helps artists understand the body's underlying structure, improving the accuracy of figure drawing.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A quick, loose sketch capturing the essential pose or movement of a figure, often completed within a short time limit, is called a
questions.explanation: Gesture drawing captures the essential movement, pose, and energy of a subject quickly, often in timed sessions of a few minutes or less.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The angular, bold style of lettering historically associated with medieval manuscripts and often used for formal or decorative headings is
questions.explanation: Gothic lettering features bold, angular strokes historically associated with medieval European manuscripts and decorative typography.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The classic lettering style featuring clean lines with serifs, historically derived from ancient Roman inscriptions, is
questions.explanation: Roman lettering, characterised by clean serif strokes, derives its style from ancient Roman inscriptional lettering.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The design and arrangement of typefaces to make written language legible, readable, and visually appealing is called
questions.explanation: Typography involves selecting, arranging, and styling text to communicate effectively and enhance the visual appeal of a design.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A simple, recognisable graphic symbol or design representing a company or organisation's identity is called a
questions.explanation: A logo is a distinctive graphic mark or symbol used to represent and identify a brand or organisation.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A large printed graphic design intended to advertise an event, product, or cause, typically displayed publicly, is called a
questions.explanation: Posters are large-format graphic designs created to promote and advertise events, products, or messages in public spaces.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The graphic design created for the outer cover of a published book, intended to attract readers and convey its content, is called a
questions.explanation: Book cover illustration combines artwork and typography to visually represent a book's content and attract potential readers.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: The graphic design applied to the container or wrapping of a product, intended to inform and attract consumers, is called
questions.explanation: Package design covers the visual and structural design of a product's packaging, balancing branding, information, and consumer appeal.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A printmaking technique involving carving a design into a linoleum block before inking and printing it is called
questions.explanation: Linocut printing involves carving a design into a sheet of linoleum, which is then inked and pressed onto paper or fabric.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A printmaking technique involving carving a design into a block of wood before inking and printing it is called
questions.explanation: Woodcut printing is one of the oldest printmaking techniques, involving carving a relief design into a block of wood.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A printmaking technique using a mesh screen and stencil to transfer ink onto a surface is called
questions.explanation: Screenprinting (silk-screening) pushes ink through a fine mesh screen, with stencilled areas blocking ink from unwanted regions.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A key consideration in effective package design is ensuring the design
options: hides all information about the product from the consumer
focuses solely on the manufacturer's internal codes
clearly communicates product information while remaining visually appealing to consumers
uses no colour or imagery of any kind
questions.explanation: Good package design balances clear communication of essential product information with visual appeal that attracts consumers.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A hand-building pottery technique involving rolling clay into long ropes and stacking them to build up a vessel's walls is called
questions.explanation: Coiling builds pottery forms by stacking and joining rope-like coils of clay, one of the oldest hand-building techniques.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A hand-building pottery technique involving rolling clay into flat sheets, which are then cut and joined to form a vessel, is called
questions.explanation: Slab building uses flat sheets of rolled clay, cut and assembled together, to construct pottery forms.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A pottery technique using a rotating wheel to shape clay by hand as it spins is called
questions.explanation: Throwing shapes clay on a spinning potter's wheel, using hand pressure to form symmetrical vessels.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A three-dimensional art technique involving the removal of material from a solid block, such as wood or stone, to reveal a form, is called
questions.explanation: Carving is a subtractive sculptural process, removing material from a solid mass to reveal the desired form.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A three-dimensional art technique involving building up and shaping a soft, pliable material, such as clay, to create a form, is called
questions.explanation: Modeling is an additive sculptural process, building up and shaping a pliable material by hand to create form.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A three-dimensional art technique involving pouring liquid material, such as molten metal or plaster, into a mould to create a form, is called
questions.explanation: Casting involves pouring a liquid material into a prepared mould, which then solidifies into the desired form.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A traditional textile technique involving tying sections of fabric before dyeing to create resist patterns is called
questions.explanation: Tie-dye creates patterns by tightly binding sections of fabric before dyeing, preventing dye from reaching the tied areas.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A traditional textile technique using wax to resist dye and create intricate patterns on fabric is called
questions.explanation: Batik applies melted wax to fabric in a design before dyeing, with the waxed areas resisting the dye to create patterns.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A traditional textile technique involving interlacing threads at right angles on a loom to create fabric is called
questions.explanation: Weaving interlaces warp and weft threads on a loom, a foundational technique for producing fabric.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A three-dimensional art technique combining found objects and diverse materials into a single unified artwork is called
questions.explanation: Assemblage art combines varied found objects and materials into a cohesive three-dimensional composition.

questions.subject: Visual Arts
questions.text: A key safety and technical consideration when firing pottery in a kiln is
options: ensuring the correct temperature is reached to properly harden and vitrify the clay
avoiding any temperature control during firing
leaving the kiln door open throughout the entire firing process
using wet, unprepared clay directly from the ground with no drying
questions.explanation: Proper kiln firing requires reaching and maintaining specific temperatures so that the clay hardens correctly and, where applicable, glazes vitrify properly.
